rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 23–26 are a parenthesis addressing the Prophet; after it, the discourse returns to its original theme, including the effects of rain and Qur'anic guidance.
rows.anchor: Verses 23-26 are parenthetical in nature and address the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain produces varied growth; likewise the Qur'an develops the righteous while exposing evil in others, as Satan instigates his followers to oppose it.
rows.anchor: Through it the abilities and potentials of the righteous develop while the evil found in others is exposed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alwān can mean types or sorts as well as colours, and it carries that broader sense in the verse's next portion too.
rows.anchor: it also means “types” and “sorts”. In the next portion of this verse also, the word is used in this very meaning.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He connects the rain imagery with 7:58: fertile land produces good vegetation, while defective land yields defective growth.
rows.anchor: In Sūrah A‘rāf, this aspect of the effects of rain is mentioned thus:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Judud is the plural of juddah, normally stripes on deer or mule backs; here it refers to large rocks or stone slabs whose bands form rows in mountains.
rows.anchor: however, here it is used for large rocks and stone tablets whose stripes or rows are found in mountains.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gharābīb is the plural of gharbīb and means jet black; it commonly intensifies the word aswad, meaning black.
rows.anchor: It means “jet black.” It is generally used to emphasize the word

rows.speaker: Linguists
rows.claim: One explanation for gharābīb preceding aswad is that it is an explicative badal; such a substitution functions as emphasis by restating the point plainly.
rows.anchor: Linguists have given different answers to this question. Some say that it is a badal (permutative) that occurs as an explication.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic reference to black mountain rocks evokes people with black hearts; the passage begins to compare the distinct uses of rock colours as well.
rows.anchor: just as there are black rocks in mountains, similarly, there are people among human beings who have black hearts;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier sūrahs use the revived earth as evidence for the Hereafter, monotheism and revelation; here the passage emphasizes providence and gratitude.
rows.anchor: attention is foremost directed to the signs found in the earth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite word ayah magnifies the sign; people need not look far because the earth under their feet is the greatest sign for them.
rows.anchor: is not defined to show its great magnitude.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God revives desolate land with rain and grain that sustains people, and supplies date palms, vines, fruit orchards and springs to nourish them.
rows.anchor: God enlivens it by sending rain

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The provisions are neither people's own work nor another being's gift; they impose gratitude to God and, as its consequence, worship of Him alone.
rows.anchor: state the obligation imposed on man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers the earth, already mentioned in the preceding verses, as the pronoun's antecedent.
rows.anchor: the antecedent of the pronoun is رضأُ earth) that is already in mention since the preceding verses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although al-ard is feminine, the masculine pronoun follows the dominant referent by the Arabic principle called ʿalā sabīl al-taghlīb.
rows.anchor: here a masculine pronoun is used to refer to it on the principle of dominant element (‘alā sabīl al-taghlīb).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic pronouns can follow the meaning a word conveys rather than its grammatical form.
rows.anchor: at times a pronoun occurs not with relation to the word but to the meaning it conveys.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun's intended referent is the fertile land: rain reaches both barren and lush areas, but only fertile land produces vegetation, as 7:58 states.
rows.anchor: This topic is discussed in Sūrah A‘rāf in the following words:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He parses “this is not the work of their hands” as a parenthetical sentence.
rows.anchor: The words اَمَو ُهْتَلِمَع ْمِهیِدْیَأُ form a parenthetical sentence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parenthesis reminds people that God, not they, brought the fruit into existence; recognizing this truth grounds gratitude, while self-entitlement breeds arrogance, polytheism and social disorder.
rows.anchor: The implication is that they should consume the fruits but always remember that they were not the ones who brought these fruits into existence;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Azwāj means both kinds or types and pairs; the verse encompasses both senses.
rows.anchor: The word اجَوْزَأُ means “types”, “kinds” and also means “pairs”. Here it encompasses both meanings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth's varied products, human differences in appearance, colour, stature and language, and unknown creations show ordered harmony under one God, excluding any partner in rule.
rows.anchor: there is a harmony of objective in its variety and accord in its discord.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since paired things serve purposes, this world must have a counterpart: otherwise it would be purposeless, which a wise Creator would not make, so the Hereafter fills that gap.
rows.anchor: when every thing occurs in pairs to achieve its purpose, it is necessary that this world should also have its counterpart;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Subḥāna declares God free from negative attributes; its contextual occasion here is clear.
rows.anchor: The word َانَحْبُس occurs to absolve someone of all negative attributes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternation of day and night is a sign of God's power, mercy, providence and oneness: daylight enables work, while darkness provides rest.
rows.anchor: the night is a great sign of God’s power, mercy, providence and monotheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The coordinated alternation shows that the world is not a clash of opposed forces; its Creator directs them to benefit creation together.
rows.anchor: This coming and going of the day and night and their harmony for the benefit of the creation is a clear testimony

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun, the day's greatest sign, follows its assigned path punctually without deviation or even a second's lapse, prompting the question whether such order could run by itself.
rows.anchor: very punctually moves along its prescribed path; it dare not deviate from this path or there lapses even a second in its punctuality.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The right answer is that this is God's planning: the world is neither accidental nor self-running, but directed by an all-powerful, dominant and all-knowing being.
rows.anchor: neither has this world come into existence accidentally nor is it being run of its own accord.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The moon is a second great sign, unable to govern itself; God has set its monthly phases until it returns to the appearance of an old palm twig.
rows.anchor: It neither controls nor governs itself. God has ordained various phases through which it passes every month.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Urjun is the branch bearing date clusters; as it dries, it takes the crescent's shape in the moon's initial and final phases.
rows.anchor: These branches after drying up assume the same shape as the one a moon has in its initial and final phases.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison rebukes foolish moon worshippers: the object they worship repeatedly wanes to a dry, crooked palm twig.
rows.anchor: This comparison is pointing to the fact that the state of the moon whom these foolish people worship
